newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia, Belarus ready for task of uniting - Yeltsin.
newsitem.headline: Russia, Belarus ready for task of uniting - Yeltsin.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin said on Thursday said Russia and its western cousin Belarus were ready to take difficult steps toward integration, predicting 1997 would be a year of "great decisions" for both nations.
"The path toward developing a community of two sovereign governments is not easy," Yeltsin said in his address to parliament. "But our governments and people are ready to carry it out to the full."
"This year will be one of great decisions for Russia and Belarus," he added. Belarus President Alexander Lukashenko will hold talks with Yeltsin in Moscow on Friday.
The two signed a pact in April 1996 forming an economic community and opening the way for developing political ties between Moscow and Minsk.
But there has been little concrete progress in furthering integration since then, partially because of Yeltsin's long illnesses from which he is only now emerging.
Last year's crisis in Minsk, which saw Russian mediators looking embarrassed and ineffectual as Lukashenko swept aside parliamentary opposition, also scarcely improved closer ties.

Yeltsin's speech on Thursday again left vague the next steps in the integration process that could, ultimately, expand Moscow's effective territorial control 500 km (350 miles) westward, back to the Polish frontier.
But the forceful appearance of the 66-year-old leader after eight months of illness signalled that Belarus was back on the Kremlin's agenda.

It seems no coincidence Moscow is taking such steps at the same time as a diplomatic offensive against NATO's plans to extend membership of the West's defence alliance to Poland and other former communist states in eastern Europe.

Yeltsin's spokesman Sergei Yastrzembsky said on Thursday he expected Lukashenko's visit to be the occasion for "serious, detailed talks on the substance of the integration process within the Commonwealth," Interfax news agency reported.

"The main thing in the first stage is bringing the legal systems closer together, unifying norms regarding rights, the creation of a unified transport and energy systems and the adjustment of borders and customs," he said.
"Then as these tasks are fulfilled, we will move toward higher levels of political integration," Yastrzembsky said.

Lukashenko said on Wednesday he foresaw joint economic, transport, economic and military structures between the two former Soviet republics. With just 10 million people in Belarus compared to 150 million in Russia, Moscow would inevitably call the shots in any joint military and other structures.
In his speech, Yeltsin did not mention an idea he first mentioned in January that the two sides should hold referendums on integration. Belarus was originally cool to the proposal.
Foreign diplomats say the talk of moving Russian borders westward is Yeltsin's strongest card in his desire to thwart NATO plans to invite new members in eastern Europe this summer.

Among the difficulties Yeltsin hinted at in his remarks on Thursday are differing outlooks between Moscow and Minsk on economic reform. Belarus has moved slowly to alter its Soviet-era planned economy.
On Tuesday, Lukashenko's Prime Minister Sergei Ling said: "Integration with Russia remains a top priority, but we will take our own path to the market economy."
